Should there be a motion to reduce the COLA within certain groups that are not included in the collective bargaining unit? Thank you, Ms. Chernoff. I'll take that question. So without knowing the motion, broadly, if the board would be considering a motion to apply a different COLA increase to certain non-certified, non-bargaining confidential positions, there would be broader structural implications for our salary scales and our employees.

So salary scale B was intentionally designed to function as a unified compensation structure for non-certified employees. Prior to fiscal year 21, LCPS operated under multiple separate salary scales, including a classified and an administrative salary scale.

And over time, that structure contributed to poor morale, perceived inconsistent treatment, and a divide between employees doing essential work across the organization. Employees on the classified scale included positions, custodians, bus drivers, electricians, HVAC technicians, nurses, and other critical support operational staff.

Often, those individuals in those positions expressed that they felt treated differently or less than, particularly when promotional movement required them crossing into separate administrative scales that included coordinators, supervisors, assistant principals, directors, supervisory positions.

Beginning in fiscal year 18 and 19, the division undertook significant work to review the classification and compensation of positions across these scales. This was the first time work of that nature was done, and this included bridging the gap between the classified and the administrative scale by adding lanes, we called them the professional lanes, to the beginning of the administrative scale.

There was a large gap between the highest level of the classified scale and the lowest level of the admin scale. And so three lanes were added before ultimately merging the classified and administrative structures into what we called the universal scale.

This was a single salary scale. And so by fiscal year 22, LCPS completed that transition, closing the divide and creating a more equitable, consistent system that supported career growth and internal alignment across all the job families.
With that context, carving out certain supervisory or school administrator roles for a different COLA increase, if that was the motion before the board, would not simply be a compensation adjustment.

it would effectively require separating those groups back out of the unified salary structure and recreating that two-tiered framework the division worked intentionally to move away from. Additionally, over time, this would also contribute to wage compression, where the pay difference between employees and their supervisors or specialists above them would narrow, making advancement into higher responsibility roles less attractive.
So in short, this is not simply a COLA decision, it was more of a structural decision with long-term implications for equity, morale, and career progression. Thank you.
